config.system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product yet. Run the proposed survey test (X1) before any investment. T1 (brand recognition in the leisure-vehicle aftermarket) is the only theory with any source support, but the support is a single trade-show remark and the one challenge found points the other way on price. T2 (EV range-preservation) has no source support at all. Hold capital in reserve for the test; do not build a product or open a direct-to-consumer channel.

frame.objective: Decide whether Eberspächer should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its B2B exhaust, heater and thermal management business, and identify the evidence that would justify that investment. The real objective is to learn whether individual buyers would pay a premium for a product Eberspächer can make and sell profitably, not to expand for its own sake.

Eberspächer's existing core is sold to vehicle manufacturers and specialist dealers, so any consumer move must reuse its engineering, brand or channels

Different route to buyers: sell direct to consumers or via online retail and installers rather than OEMs and specialist dealers
Different customer group: target a niche such as overlanders, campervan converters, off-grid users or EV owners needing cabin or battery warmth

T1.claim: Individual owners of campervans and caravans already seek out Eberspächer heaters because the brand is known from installed units, so a consumer offer could be built on existing recognition and aftermarket fitting rather than a new product.
T1.who_benefits: Camper and caravan owners who want reliable heat off-grid; Eberspächer, which could sell replacement and upgrade units into an existing installed base.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Owners who have used a heater in a previous vehicle trust the brand and choose it again when they buy or refit a leisure vehicle, so brand memory rather than price drives the choice.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Eberspächer sells through its existing products and specialist fitters, earning margin on heater units, installation kits and service parts sold to people who already know the brand.
assumptions: Trade-show interest from private buyers reflects real purchasing intent, not curiosity
Replacement and refit demand exists in the installed base at a meaningful volume
Existing heater units can be sold to private buyers without a product redesign
predictions: Share of leisure-vehicle buyers naming Eberspächer unprompted is higher than for comparable heater brands
Aftermarket enquiries and replacement sales rise where a dealer or fitter offers installation
Owners of older installed units request service or upgrades at a measurable rate
T1.first_claim: Individual owners of campervans and caravans already seek out Eberspächer heaters because the brand is known from installed units, so a consumer offer could be built on existing recognition and aftermarket fitting rather than a new product.

T2.claim: Electric-vehicle owners will pay a premium for a heater that protects range and battery in cold weather, so a consumer product built around range preservation, not brand memory, could earn a margin that the current OEM-sold units do not.
T2.who_benefits: Owners of battery electric vehicles in cold climates, who lose driving range when cabin or battery heating draws on the traction battery; Eberspächer, which has electric heater and thermal management engineering.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: When range anxiety is the main barrier to EV use in winter, a buyer who values extra range in cold conditions will pay for a product that cuts that loss, and the value is measurable in kilometres.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Eberspächer sells an aftermarket or accessory electric heater or pre-conditioning unit, or licenses its engineering to an accessory maker, capturing margin on a product priced against the range it saves.
assumptions: Cold-weather range loss is large enough that owners notice and value its reduction
Aftermarket fitting of a heater into an EV is technically and legally feasible for consumers
Owners prefer to buy a fitted range-saving product over relying on the OEM's own pre-conditioning
predictions: Stated willingness to pay is higher among EV owners in cold regions than in warm regions
Owners who quote range loss figures are more likely to buy a range-preserving accessory

T2.first_claim: Electric-vehicle owners will pay a premium for a heater that protects range and battery in cold weather, so a consumer product built around range preservation, not brand memory, could earn a margin that the current OEM-sold units do not.

assessments.does_not_show: This is a trade-show exhibitor's remark, reported by the company's own newsroom. It shows recognition among some visitors at one fair, not market share, unprompted brand choice across the population, purchase intent, or how many installed units exist or would need replacing.

assessments.quote: Clammy fingers in the morning are a thing of the past. With an Eberspächer pre-heater, you can look forward to getting into a pleasantly warm car with fully de-iced windows.
assessments.does_not_show: The page sells comfort and de-icing for conventional cars, not range or battery protection for electric vehicles. It says nothing about EV owners, range loss, willingness to pay, or whether an aftermarket EV heater is feasible. T2 is untested by any source I have read.

assessments.quote: Caravan and motorhome owners are tempted to purchase these units because of the huge price difference between them and the name brand equivalents.
assessments.does_not_show: This is an Australian RV magazine's editorial view, not a survey of buyers. It does not measure how many owners buy cheap heaters, whether price outweighs brand for Eberspächer's buyers in Europe, or the size of any premium. It contradicts only the claim that brand alone drives choice, and it does not address installed-base replacement.

X1.name: Brand recall and price-premium survey with EV range cohort
X1.method: Online discrete-choice survey with two cohorts. Cohort A: owners of campervans, caravans or motorhomes who have used or considered an auxiliary heater, measuring unprompted brand recall and choice between a named Eberspächer-type heater, an unbranded heater, and a cheap import at several price points. Cohort B: battery-electric vehicle owners in cold regions, shown a cold-weather range-loss message, then asked about willingness to buy an aftermarket range-preserving heater at several price points. A landing-page pre-order intent step is included in Cohort B to test real intent against stated intent.
X1.sample: Proposed: Cohort A n=400 leisure-vehicle owners in Germany via an online panel quota-matched on vehicle type. Cohort B n=200 BEV owners in Germany, Norway or Sweden. Estimated cost EUR 12,000 to 15,000 for panel and analysis, plus EUR 3,000 to 5,000 for the landing-page intent step (estimated, not quoted).
X1.measure: Cohort A: unprompted brand recall rate; share choosing the branded heater at a stated price premium over the unbranded option. Cohort B: share stating intent to buy at each price, and share converting to a refundable pre-order deposit click.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Unprompted recall of Eberspächer among leisure owners is high, and a meaningful share will choose the branded heater over an unbranded one at a premium, with the premium holding across price points.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Stated and pre-order intent among BEV owners is high at prices that reflect range saved, and that intent is higher than among leisure owners' choice of a branded heater.

X1.decision_rule: Keep T1 as a live option only if at least 25% of Cohort A names the brand unprompted AND at least 30% of those who choose a heater pick the branded option at a 15% premium over the unbranded option. Keep T2 only if at least 20% of Cohort B shows intent at the proposed price AND at least 5% click the pre-order step. If neither threshold is met in its cohort, reject that theory for a consumer launch. Both thresholds are analyst proposals, not derived from data.

revisions.reason: No change. SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not counted as evidence. Its mechanism (installation friction affecting deposits within a recruited group) does not test brand recognition or willingness to pay a premium, so T1 stays uncertain. The current evidence for T1 remains the trade-show remark, and the RV Daily editorial that cuts against it on price.

No change. SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not counted as evidence. It concerns installation friction for parking heaters among camper owners, not EV range preservation, so it does not bear on T2. T2 remains untested: none of the sources I read address EV owners or range loss.

Suppose SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE were real. It would show that, among 400 recruited camper and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater, a mobile fitting offer produced 72 deposits against 32 for a dealer-workshop offer at identical price and product. That bears on installation friction, not on brand recognition or a willingness to pay a premium, so it would not change T1's claim. It is SIMULATED and I do not count it as evidence. T1 stays uncertain until survey X1 is run.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product or a direct-to-consumer channel now. Default to no expansion for the present, and fund only the proposed 10-week survey test (X1, about EUR 18,000 estimated) to decide whether a consumer proposition is worth building. Public evidence shows some consumer recognition of Eberspächer heaters in the leisure-vehicle and boat aftermarket, but nothing shows that buyers would pay a premium for a dedicated consumer product, and nothing I read addresses electric-vehicle range.
final.target_customer: Provisionally, owners of campervans, caravans and motorhomes who have used or are considering an auxiliary heater, because that is where the one piece of recognition evidence points. This is a hypothesis to test, not a finding. EV owners are an untested alternative.
final.value_proposition: Not yet defined. The candidate is a branded, professionally fitted auxiliary heater for leisure vehicles priced against cheaper imports. Whether the brand justifies a premium is the open question the test must answer.
final.next_action: Run test X1 as proposed: an online discrete-choice survey of about 400 leisure-vehicle owners in Germany measuring unprompted brand recall and choice at price premiums, plus a 200-person BEV cohort on range-preservation intent. Proceed to a product or channel decision only if the T1 threshold is met (at least 25% unprompted recall and at least 30% of heater choosers picking the brand at a 15% premium). Otherwise drop T1 for a consumer launch. Do not spend on redesign until then.
final.uncertainty: High. Sample, budget, timing and thresholds are my proposals and estimates, not company figures. I could not find Eberspächer's consumer sales volumes, margins, aftermarket channel size, installed-base numbers, pricing or contract and distribution detail; these are probably non-public. The only recognition evidence is one company-published trade-show remark, and the one challenge is an Australian RV editorial, not a survey. T2 has no supporting source. The simulated result was not treated as evidence and changes nothing here. Six searches remain unused.
would_change_if: Survey X1 shows under 25% unprompted recall among leisure-vehicle owners, which would reject T1 for a consumer launch
Brand premium under 15% against unbranded heaters, which would favour a product redesign or licensing route
Non-public company data showing a large existing private-owner aftermarket base, which would favour the aftermarket route
Evidence that EV owners in cold regions quantify and pay for range loss at prices that cover an accessory product, which would make T2 the favoured theory
Credible independent evidence that installation friction drives purchase at scale, shifting value toward fitting services
An independent market study showing the leisure heater aftermarket is price-driven, which would weaken a premium brand proposition

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE is a SIMULATED, hypothetical result. It is not real data, so I do not count it as evidence for or against T1. Even if it were real, it would bear on how installation friction affects choice within a recruited group of camper owners, which is a mechanism question rather than a test of brand recognition or willingness to pay a premium. It would not change T1's claim. T1 stays uncertain until the proposed survey X1 is run.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
